units.translation: the fate of the clear-voiced nightingale
such mournful woes I utter, shrill, heavy, tear-falling
and from the battlements a shower of stones comes
you will have no stone to pick up from the ground
In both places in M Λίλαιος [Lilaios], which Lehrs corrected, de stud. Aristarchi p. 297 ed. sec.
with which Abreschius compared Eur. Or. 1077 ὦ δῶμα πατρὸς καὶ μέγας πλούτου λιμήν [O house of my father and great harbor of wealth].
O Persian land and great harbor of wealth
and nowhere a harbor from evils
O house of my father and great harbor of wealth

where λίμναν [lake] is written in the books, which is correctly read in another fragment (271) in Arist. Ran. 1297 Ἑρμᾶν μὲν πρόγονον τίομεν γένος οἱ περὶ λίμναν [we honor Hermes as ancestor, the race around the lake].
at the narrow gates of the lake
leaving the Delian lake and the rocky islet
cast into the purple lake the black-yoked ruin
the all-nourishing lake of the Ethiopians
we honor Hermes as ancestor, the race around the lake
a beggar, wretched, dying of hunger
very many died by thirst and hunger
killing with hunger those who are too numerous
the hunger that dwells with hateful darkness (thus Scaliger for δυσφιλής κότῳ [hateful wrath])
and the orphaned ones are oppressed by fasting hunger
if hunger or thirst (δίψησις [thirst] Wellauer) or retention of urine holds them
where commonly λίνα δέ [linen things], the Paris codex has λινάδες [linen things].
"linen things, pitch, and long cords of raw flax"
having crossed the strait on a raft bound with cords

Correctly the scholiast: ἐν περιφράσει τὸν κλωστὸν λίνον [in periphrasis the spun thread]. The same from Euripides is cited by Pollux 7, 31 λίνου κλωστήρα περιφέρει λαβών [carrying a spindle of flax].
I fall with torn linen garments or a Sidonian veil
saving the spun thread of flax from the deep (λίνον [flax] M, recent manuscripts; λίνῳ [with flax] in Clem. Al. Strom. 2 p. 504.)
linen-winged, it found the vehicles of sailors

where the scholiast: ἡ ναῦς παρ᾿ ὅσον τρυπῶντες τὰς ναῦς σπάρτοις αὐτὰς συνέρραπτον, καὶ τὸ παρ ' Ὁμήρῳ [the ship, inasmuch as they bored holes in the ships and sewed them together with cords, and the phrase in Homer] (Od. 14, 383) “ νῆας ἀκειόμενον ” [mending the ships] means συρράπτοντες [sewing together].
the oar of the linen-sewn ship and its course (thus I corrected for δόμος [house]) keeping off the sea from the timber
the ship, inasmuch as they bored holes in the ships and sewed them together with cords, and the phrase in Homer
mending the ships means sewing together
to entreat earnestly, to press with prayers
to entreat earnestly, to press with prayers
I will entreat the greatly hated one
